title: Training Webpage Template: User Guide
text:
Welcome to the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template User Guide!
The SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template helps training organisers across SciLifeLab create consistent, reusable and FAIR training websites. No programming is needed: you fill in a few text files with information about your training, write your materials in Markdown, and the website is built and published for you.

How a training website is organised
Each training gets one website with two parts:

A landing page with general information about the training and links to every time it is given.
A training instance for each time the training is given, with its own overview, schedule, materials and practical information.



What this guide covers
This guide takes you step by step from an empty template to a published, citable training website. It covers how to:

create your own copy of the template and preview it on your computer;
set up the landing page;
create a training instance and add your materials;
prepare your training materials for publication, citation, and reuse following FAIR principles.

No prior experience with Git, Python or Quarto is needed. Start with Set up your training and follow it once from beginning to end. After that, you can go straight to the chapter you need.



This User Guide is maintained by the SciLifeLab Training Hub.
Questions, problems or ideas for improving the guide or the template? Open an issue or email us at training@scilifelab.se.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.1 Install the software
This chapter takes you through everything you need to do once, at the start, to get your own training website. You will create your own copy of the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template, publish it as a website, and set it up on your computer so you can edit it.
This is the only part of the guide you do just once, and takes about an hour. Take your time: each step explains what you are doing and why, and what you should see when it worked.
Once you are done, the next chapter, Regular workflow, shows the few steps you repeat every time you update your website.
To work with the template, you need a free GitHub account and four free programs. If you already have some of them, you can skip those.
Install each program with the default settings. Then open Visual Studio Code (VS Code) once, to check that it starts.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.2 Create your repository
A repository is the folder on GitHub that holds everything for your training: the information about it, the materials, and the website. You create your own repository as a copy of the template. The template itself stays unchanged, so you can’t break anything for others.

Open the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template on GitHub.
In the top-right corner of the page, click the green Use this template button and select Create a new repository.



Fill in the form:

Turn Include all branches on. This is required: the template keeps the landing page and each training instance in separate branches (you will learn about these later), and you need all of them.
Under Owner, select the GitHub organisation or account where the repository should live, for example SciLifeLab-Training, NBISweden, or your personal account.
Under Repository name, enter a short name in lowercase, with hyphens instead of spaces, for example introduction-to-r. The name becomes part of your website address, so choose it carefully.
Under Visibility, choose Public, so participants can see the website and materials.

Click Create repository.


GitHub now opens your new repository. Check the name at the top of the page: it should be the name you just chose, not the template’s name.







TipWorking with others? Add collaborators (optional)





If other people will help develop or maintain the training, give them access to the repository. You can also do this later.

In your repository, click Settings. 
Under Access in the menu on the left, click Collaborators and teams. 
Click Add people or Add teams.
Search for the person or team, choose a role, and click Add. 

The options you see depend on whether the repository belongs to you or to an organisation, and on your permissions in that organisation.




Done when: you see your own repository on GitHub, with the name you chose.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.3 Publish your website
Your new repository already contains a ready-made copy of the template website, and GitHub usually publishes it and sets it up by itself. In this step you check two settings, and add your website link to your repository’s main page.

Check that your website is online

In your repository, click Settings, then Pages in the menu on the left. 
At the top of the page, look for Your site is live at, followed by your website address. It looks like https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY-NAME/, with your organisation (or user name) and repository name filled in. 

For now, your website shows the template’s example content. It changes to your own content the first time you upload a change.






NoteDon’t see “Your site is live at”?





Sometimes GitHub doesn’t switch on publishing by itself. You can do it yourself:

On the same page, under Source, choose Deploy from a branch.
Under Branch, choose gh-pages and / (root), and click Save. 
Wait a minute or two and refresh the page. Your site is live at now appears at the top.






Check that your website can be updated
Every time you upload a change, GitHub runs a small automatic process that rebuilds your website. This process needs permission to update the website.

Click Settings, then Actions → General in the menu on the left.
Scroll down to Workflow permissions, and check that Read and write permissions is selected. 







NoteIs “Read repository contents and packages permissions” selected instead?





Select Read and write permissions and click Save.
If you can’t select it because the option is greyed out, your organisation controls this setting. Ask an administrator of the organisation to allow it for your repository.





Add the website link to your repository
Show the website address on your repository’s main page, so you can always find your website quickly:

Click the Code tab to go back to the repository’s main page. 
On the right-hand side, next to About, click the gear icon ⚙️.
Tick Use your GitHub Pages website and click Save changes. 


Done when: the website link appears under About, and clicking it opens the template website.

title: 2  Set up your training
section: 2.4 Open the repository on your computer
text:
2.4 Open the repository on your computer
So far, your repository only exists on GitHub. To edit it, you make a copy on your computer. This is called cloning.
Working on a copy has a big advantage: nothing you change is visible to anyone else until you decide to upload it. You can try things out, look at the result, and undo mistakes, all safely on your own computer.

On your repository’s main page on GitHub, click the green Code button, make sure HTTPS is selected, and copy the address.

Open VS Code and click Clone Git Repository on the start screen. If you don’t see it, open View → Command Palette, type Git: Clone and press Enter.

Paste the HTTPS address you copied and press Enter.
Choose where to save the repository on your computer, for example a folder called GitHub inside Documents, and click Select as Repository Destination. 
When VS Code asks whether to open the repository, click Open.

The files and folders of your repository now appear in the Explorer panel on the left side of VS Code. Throughout this guide, you open files by clicking them there.
If VS Code suggests installing recommended extensions, click Install. They help VS Code understand the files used in the template.







TipPrefer the terminal?





cd ~/Documents/GitHub
git clone https://github.com/ORGANISATION/REPOSITORY-NAME.git
Then open the new folder in VS Code with File → Open Folder…




✓ Done when: you see your repository’s files in the Explorer panel in VS Code.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.5 Set up the environment
Your website is built by a few small Python scripts that come with the template. These scripts need one extra Python package. In this step you install it in a separate, self-contained environment inside your repository folder, so it doesn’t interfere with anything else on your computer.
You only do this once for each repository. You don’t need to understand the commands: copy each one exactly as shown.

Open a terminal
A terminal is a window where you type commands. In VS Code, choose Terminal → New Terminal.

The terminal opens at the bottom of the window, already inside your repository folder.
To run a command from this guide, copy it, paste it into the terminal, and press Enter.



Check the software
First, check that Git, Python and Quarto were installed correctly. Run these commands one by one:

macOS and LinuxWindows


git --version
python3 --version
quarto --version


git --version
python --version
quarto --version



Each command should print a version number, for example Python 3.12.4 (see image above). If one says command not found, install that program again, restart VS Code, and try again.


Create the environment
Run these three commands one by one. The last one can take a minute.

macOS and LinuxWindows


python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt


python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt



The first command creates the environment, the second switches it on, and the third installs what the scripts need. When the environment is switched on, the terminal line starts with (.venv):
(.venv) username@computer introduction-to-r %



Let VS Code switch on the environment
The environment has to be switched on each time you open a new terminal. You can let VS Code do that for you:

Press Cmd+Shift+P (macOS) or Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows and Linux).
Type Python: Select Interpreter and press Enter.
Choose the option that shows .venv.


From now on, every new terminal you open in this repository starts with the environment switched on.

Done when: a new terminal (Terminal → New Terminal) starts with (.venv).

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
You’re all set!
Your training has its own repository and website, and your computer is ready to edit it. You won’t need to repeat any of these steps for this training.
Continue with Regular workflow to make your first change and see it appear on your website.



This User Guide is maintained by the SciLifeLab Training Hub.
Questions, problems or ideas for improving the guide or the template? Open an issue or email us at training@scilifelab.se.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.1 Open your training
This chapter shows the steps you repeat every time you work on your training website: open your training, preview it, make your changes, and publish them.
The steps are always the same, whether you change a date, add a team member or write a new page of materials. After doing them once or twice they quickly become routine. The cheat sheet at the end of this chapter lists all of them on one screen, for when you just need a reminder.
Each time you start working, open your repository in VS Code and make sure you have the latest version.
Screenshot: VS Code status bar with the branch name and the Synchronize Changes arrows.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
Open VS Code. It usually reopens the repository you worked on last. If not, choose File → Open Recent, or File → Open Folder… and select your repository folder.
Get the latest version. If you work together with others, they may have uploaded changes since you last worked. In the bottom-left corner of VS Code, click the circular arrows next to the branch name (Synchronize Changes). This downloads their changes to your computer.



Which part of your website are you working on?
The bottom-left corner of VS Code also shows the branch you are working on. Your repository keeps each part of your website in its own branch:

main: the landing page.
release- followed by four digits, for example release-2605: one training instance, here the one in May 2026.

Before you start editing, check that you are on the branch you want to change. You will learn how to switch branches in the chapter Training instances. For your first change below, stay on main.
Screenshot: VS Code status bar showing the branch name main.
✓ Done when: your repository is open in VS Code, and the bottom-left corner shows the branch you want to work on.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.2 Preview your website
A preview shows your website in your web browser while you work on it, before anything is published. The preview runs on your own computer, so only you can see it. This lets you check every change before your collaborators or participants see it.
To start the preview, open a terminal (Terminal → New Terminal) and run:
quarto preview
Quarto now builds your website. After a few seconds, it opens in your web browser. If it doesn’t open by itself, copy the address shown in the terminal, for example http://localhost:4268/, and paste it into your browser.
fig-alt=“Landing page displayed locally in a web browser using Quarto preview.”
Keep the preview running while you work. Each time you save a file, the preview updates by itself.

To run other commands while the preview is running, open a second terminal with Terminal → New Terminal. The terminal running the preview is busy.
To stop the preview when you are done, click in the terminal where it runs and press Ctrl+C.







TipAnother way to start the preview: the Preview button





When a page file (ending in .qmd) is open in VS Code, you can also click the Preview button in the top-right corner of the editor. The website then opens inside VS Code. To see it in your browser instead, click Open in Browser.
Screenshot: VS Code showing the Preview button.









NoteThe preview stops with “Include directive failed”





This can happen the first time you preview a training instance with a newer version of Quarto. Run this command once, then start the preview again:
python scripts/render_course.py



✓ Done when: your website is open in your browser.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.3 Make a change
Almost everything on your website comes from the files in the data folder: the title, dates, team, schedule, and so on. You change your website by changing these files. You don’t need to touch any code.
As a first change, try changing the title of your training:

In the Explorer panel, open the data folder and click course.yml.
Find the line:
title: "Training title"
Change the text between the quotation marks, for example:
title: "My first training website"
Save the file with Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux).

The new title appears at the top of the preview in your browser.
Screenshot: Updated title in the preview.






Tip



The data files are sensitive to layout. Keep the quotation marks, and keep the spaces at the start of each line exactly as they are. If the preview shows an error after you save, check those first. The lines starting with # are explanations: they don’t appear on the website.


✓ Done when: the preview shows your new title.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.4 Commit and push your changes
Your change is now saved on your computer, but nobody else can see it yet. Publishing it takes two steps, both in VS Code’s Source Control panel:

Commit: save a version of your changes, with a short description of what you changed. Each commit is kept, so you can always see what changed and when.
Push: upload your commits to GitHub. GitHub then updates your website automatically.


Click the Source Control icon on the left side of VS Code. Your changed file, data/course.yml, is listed under Changes.

Screenshot: Source Control panel showing the changed file.

Hover over the file and click the + (Stage Changes). This tells VS Code to include the file in your commit. Files you don’t stage stay on your computer only.
In the Message box at the top, describe your change, for example Change the training title.
Click Commit.

Screenshot: message box and Commit button.

Click Sync Changes to push your commit to GitHub.

Screenshot: Sync Changes button.






Note



The first time you push, VS Code asks you to sign in to GitHub. Follow the instructions in your browser, then return to VS Code.








TipChanged something by mistake?





Before you commit, you can undo all changes to a file: in the Source Control panel, hover over the file and click the curved arrow (Discard Changes). The file goes back to how it was at your last commit.



✓ Done when: the Source Control panel shows no more changes.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.5 Check the published website
After you push, GitHub rebuilds and publishes your website by itself. This usually takes one or two minutes. You can follow it on GitHub:

Open your repository on GitHub and click the Actions tab.
Wait until both of these show a green checkmark:

deploy-landing (or deploy-instance, when you changed a training instance): builds your website;
pages build and deployment: publishes it.

A yellow dot means it is still running.

Screenshot: Actions tab with deploy-landing and pages build and deployment both green.

Open your website with the link under About on your repository’s main page.







Tip



Still seeing the old version? Wait a minute and refresh the page. Browsers sometimes show an older copy for a short while.
A red cross in the Actions tab means something went wrong. Click it to see the error message, or see the cheat sheet below.


✓ Done when: your published website shows your change.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:

You now know the routine for every change. Continue with:

Landing page: describe your training on the landing page.
Training instances: create the website for each time your training is given.
FAIRification: make your training citable and findable.

title: 4  Repository structure

The template also contains additional branches used for course instances and publication. You will work with these later in the guide.

2605 │ └── May 2026 course website

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.3 Branches






Note



The course website uses different branches for different purposes:

main contains the course landing page and general course information.
Course instance branches contain the training materials for individual course runs.
gh-pages contains the published website and is managed automatically.

You should not edit the gh-pages branch directly.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.1 Remove the template banner
The landing page introduces your course and provides visitors with the information they need to decide whether they want to register for your course or access a course instance.
The figure below shows the main sections of the landing page and the terminology used throughout this guide.
In the following sections, you will find how to:
Each section in this chapter explains which file to edit and provides step-by-step instructions.
At the end of each section, you will also find a Quick reference box summarising the most important changes. These boxes show you at a glance which file to edit and what to change, and can be useful when you return to the guide after you are already familiar with the individual steps.
The yellow banner at the top of the landing page provides a link to this User Guide. It is included to help you set up and customise the template and is not intended to remain on your course website.
Once you are ready to use the template for your own course, you can remove the banner.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
In the main branch, open index.qmd.
Locate the following line:

{{< include _sections/template-banner.qmd >}}

Delete this line. The banner will no longer appear when the landing page is rendered.







Note



You do not need to delete the file _sections/template-banner.qmd. Leaving the file in the repository will not affect your course website as long as it is no longer included in index.qmd.
If you do want to delete the file:

VS Code: Right-click the file and select Delete.
GitHub Desktop: Open the repository, locate the file, click the three dots (⋮), and choose Delete file.




 Quick reference 
 Remove the template banner 








To…
File
Edit




Remove the template banner
index.qmd
Delete the line that includes _sections/template-banner.qmd.

title: 5  Landing page
section: 5.2 Hero: Change the course title and subtitle
text:
5.2 Hero: Change the course title and subtitle
The hero is the large banner at the top of the landing page. It is the first thing visitors see when they open your course website and contains the course title, subtitle, logos, and ‘current course instance’ and ‘registration’ action buttons.

5.2.1 Change the course title

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file hero.qmd.
Locate the following lines:

:::{.hero__title}
Course title
:::

Replace Course title with the title of your course.



5.2.2 Change the course subtitle

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file hero.qmd.
Locate the following lines:

:::{.hero__subtitle}
Course subtitle
:::

Replace Course subtitle with a one-line description of your course.







Tip



Keep the subtitle to one sentence and start with an action verb such as Learn, Understand, Explore, Build, or Apply.
For example:

Learn how to apply open science practices throughout the research lifecycle.




 Quick reference 
 Change course title and subtitle 








To…
File
Edit




Change the course title
_sections/hero.qmd
Replace the text between :::{.hero__title} and :::.


Change the course subtitle
_sections/hero.qmd
Replace the text between :::{.hero__subtitle} and :::.

title: 5  Landing page
section: 5.3 Hero: Add or remove a logo
text:
5.3 Hero: Add or remove a logo
The logos displayed in the hero banner represent the organisations associated with your course. You can add additional logos, remove existing ones, or replace them with your own.

5.3.1 Add a logo

Save your logo as a PNG or SVG file.







Tip



If possible, use a white version of your logo so that it contrasts well with the dark background of the hero banner.



In the main branch, open the img folder, then the logos folder.
Copy your logo file into the folder.

VS Code: Drag and drop the file into the folder.
GitHub Desktop: Click Add file, then Upload files.

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file hero.qmd.
Locate the following block:

<div class="hero__brand-item">
  <img src="img/logos/SciLifeLab_Logotype_NEG.png"
       alt="SciLifeLab"
       class="hero__partner-logo">
</div>

Copy the entire block and paste it directly below the existing one.
Replace only the src and alt values with those for your own logo.

For example:
<div class="hero__brand-item">
  <img src="img/logos/your-logo-file.png"
       alt="Your organisation"
       class="hero__partner-logo">
</div>


5.3.2 Remove a logo

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file hero.qmd.
Locate the logo block you want to remove.

For example:
<div class="hero__brand-item">
  <img src="img/logos/SciLifeLab_Logotype_NEG.png"
       alt="SciLifeLab"
       class="hero__partner-logo">
</div>

Delete the entire <div class="hero__brand-item">...</div> block.
OPTIONAL: If you no longer need the logo image, you can also delete it from the img/logos folder.

VS Code: Right-click the file and select Delete.
GitHub Desktop: Open the repository, locate the file, click the three dots (⋮), and choose Delete file.



 Quick reference 
 Add or remove a logo 








To…
File
Edit




Add a logo
img/logos
Copy your logo image (.png or .svg) into the folder.


Display a logo on the landing page
_sections/hero.qmd
Copy an existing <div class="hero__brand-item">...</div> block and update the src and alt attributes.


Remove a logo from the landing page
_sections/hero.qmd
Delete the corresponding <div class="hero__brand-item">...</div> block.


Delete an unused logo file (optional)

Delete the logo image if it is no longer needed.

title: 5  Landing page
section: 5.4 Hero: Configure the current course instance and registration action buttons
text:
5.4 Hero: Configure the current course instance and registration action buttons
The hero can display two action buttons:

Take me to the current course instance links visitors to the current published course instance.
Register now links visitors to the course registration page.

You can change these buttons’ links and text, or hide them when they are not needed.

5.4.1 Add a link to the current course instance button

In the main branch, open the data folder and then the file instances.yml.
Locate the course instance with:

status: current

Update slug, label, instance_url, and sort_key to match the current course instance.







Important



The values of slug and instance_url must match!


For example:
instances:
  - slug: "0000"
    label: "May 2026"
    status: current
    visible: true
    show_in_hero: true
    instance_url: "./0000/"
    registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"
    sort_key: 200000
For a course instance taught in May 2026, this could become:
instances:
  - slug: "2605"
    label: "May 2026"
    status: current
    visible: true
    show_in_hero: true
    instance_url: "./2605/"
    registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"
    sort_key: 202605






Tip



In this template, each course instance is generated from a repository branch and is named using the year and month in which the instance is taught.
For example, a course taught in May 2026 uses 2605. Its relative course instance URL is therefore ./2605/.




5.4.2 Add a link to the registration button
If registration for your training is open, you can display the Register now button and link it directly to your registration page.

In the main branch, open the data folder and then the file instances.yml.
Locate the course instance with:

status: current

Find registration_url:

registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"

Replace the example URL with the URL of your course registration page.

For example:
registration_url: "https://your-registration-page.example"


5.4.3 Hide the current course instance button
If you don’t have a current course instance (e.g. if the course is self-paced or dormant), you can hide the current course instance button.

In data/instances.yml, locate the current course instance and change:

show_in_hero: true
to:
show_in_hero: false
The current course instance can remain in instances.yml; it will simply no longer be displayed as a button in the hero.


5.4.4 Hide the registration button
If the registration for your training is closed, or if the training doesn’t require registration, you can hide the registration button.

In data/instances.yml, change:

registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"
to:
registration_url: ""
An empty registration_url tells the template not to display the registration button.


5.4.5 Change action button text
You can also change the text displayed inside either action button without changing where the button links.

In the main branch, open the data folder and then the file ui.yml.
Locate:

hero_view_current_label: Take me to the current course instance
hero_registration_open_label: Register now

Replace the text after the colon with the text you want to display.

For example:
hero_view_current_label: View the latest course
hero_registration_open_label: Register for the course
Do not change the names hero_view_current_label or hero_registration_open_label. Only change the text after the colon.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.5 Course information cards: edit text
The information cards below the hero banner provide key information about your course, including the course content, learning outcomes, topics covered, keywords, course founders, and contributors. Each card can be edited independently.

5.5.1 Change the course content card

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file top-cards.qmd.
Find the Course content card.
Under:

:::{.card-copy}
Description of the content of the course

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit...
replace the example text with a description of your course.






Tip



Keep the course description concise and focus on what the course covers. Around 10 sentences is usually enough.




5.5.2 Change the learning outcomes card

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file top-cards.qmd.
Find the Learning outcomes card.
Under:

:::{.card-copy}
1. Learning outcome 1
2. Learning outcome 2
3. Learning outcome 3
replace the example learning outcomes with the learning outcomes for your course.






Tip



Learning outcomes should describe what participants will be able to do after completing the course.
For guidance on writing learning outcomes, see the SciLifeLab Training Hub resource on writing learning outcomes.




5.5.3 Change the keywords card

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file top-cards.qmd.
Find the Keywords card.
Under:

:::{.card-copy}
- Keyword 1
- Keyword 2
replace the example keywords with keywords that describe your course.






Tip



Around four or five keywords is usually enough. Choose short terms that describe the main subject areas of the course.




5.5.4 Change the topics covered cards

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file top-cards.qmd.
Find the Topics covered card.
Under:

:::{.card-copy}
- Topic 1
- Topic 2
replace the example topics with the main topics covered by your course.






Tip



Use short phrases rather than complete sentences. Aim to give visitors a quick overview of the main subjects covered by the course.




5.5.5 Change the course founders card
The Course founders card can be used to acknowledge the people who originally developed or established the course.

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file bottom-cards.qmd.
Find the Course founders card.
Under:

:::{.card-copy}
- Course founder 1
- Course founder 2
replace the example names with the names of the course founders.


5.5.6 Change the course contributors
The Contributors card can be used to acknowledge people who have contributed to the development or maintenance of the course.

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file bottom-cards.qmd.
Find the Contributors card.
Under:

:::{.card-copy}
- Contributor 1
- Contributor 2
replace the example names with the names of the course contributors.

title: 5  Landing page
section: 5.6 Change the course instance banner image
text:
5.6 Change the course instance banner image
The All course instances banner contains a decorative image alongside the links to the available course instances. You can replace this image with an image that represents your course.

5.6.1 1. Add your image

In the main branch, open the img folder and then the images folder.
Add the image you want to use, for example:

my-course-banner.jpg






Tip



A landscape-oriented image works best because the image is cropped automatically to fill the available area.




5.6.2 2. Update the image path

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file instances-band.qmd.
Locate:

  <img src="img/images/navet-band.png" alt="" class="instances-band__image">

Replace img/images/navet-band.png with the path to your image, for example:

<img src="img/images/my-course-banner.jpg" alt="" class="instances-band__image">
The image is decorative, so the alt attribute can remain empty.






Tip



Check how the image appears at different browser widths. The banner automatically crops the image to fill the available space.
If the most important part of your image is being cropped, you can adjust its position in styles.css. Find:
.instances-band__image {
  object-fit: cover;
  object-position: center;
}
Change object-position to move the visible part of the image. For example:
object-position: center top;
or:
object-position: 30% center;



Quick reference
 Change the course instance banner image

File
Edit




Add a new banner image
img/images/
Add your course image to this folder.


Change the banner image
_sections/instances-band.qmd
Replace img/images/navet-band.png with the path to your image.


(Optional) Adjust how the image is cropped
styles.css
Change object-position under .instances-band__image.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.7 Manage course instances
The All course instances banner provides links to the different published instances of your course. This allows visitors to access the current course instance, as well as previous course instances that you choose to make available.
Course instances are managed in data/instances.yml. The instance marked as current is also used for the Take me to the current course instance action button in the hero. Some of the settings described in this section therefore overlap with the instructions for configuring the hero buttons.






Important




Each course instance must have a unique slug. Do not use the same slug for more than one instance!
Only one course instance should be marked as:

status: current

The instance marked as current determines which course instance is treated as the current course throughout the landing page, including the link used by the hero action button. See Mark a course instance as current for instructions.




5.7.1 Add a new course instance

In the main branch, open the data folder and then the file instances.yml.
Copy a full existing course instance entry.
Paste the copied entry under instances:.
Update the slug, label, instance_url and sort key values to describe the new course instance.

For example, for a new course instance taught in November 2026:
- slug: "2611"
  label: "November 2026"
  status: current
  visible: true
  show_in_hero: true
  instance_url: "./2611/"
  registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"
  sort_key: 202611


5.7.2 Mark a course instance as current

In the main branch, open the data folder and then the file instances.yml.
Find the previous current instance.
Change:

status: current
to:
status: previous

Set the new current instance to:

status: current
For example:
instances:
  - slug: "2611"
    label: "November 2026"
    status: current
    visible: true
    show_in_hero: true
    instance_url: "./2611/"
    registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"
    sort_key: 202611

  - slug: "2605"
    label: "May 2026"
    status: previous
    visible: true
    show_in_hero: false
    instance_url: "./2605/"
    registration_url: ""
    sort_key: 202605


5.7.3 Show or hide a previous instance in the All course instances banner

In the main branch, open the data folder and then the file instances.yml.
To display an instance in the banner:

visible: true

To hide an instance in the banner:

visible: false
Hiding an instance does not delete it from instances.yml. It simply prevents it from being displayed in the banner.






Important



The instance marked as:
status: current
must always remain:
visible: true
Do not hide the current course instance by setting visible: false. If you do not want the current instance to appear as a button in the hero, use:
show_in_hero: false
instead.




5.7.4 Change the course instance name displayed in the banner

In the main branch, open the data folder and then the file instances.yml.
Change the value for label For example:

label: "May 2026"
can be changed to:
label: "November 2026"
Changing the label only changes the text visitors see. It does not change the course instance URL.


5.7.5 Change the order of course instances
The sort_key determines the chronological order of the course instances.

In the main branch, open the data folder and then the file instances.yml.
Change the value for sort_key. Use the format

YYYYMM
For example:
sort_key: 202605
represents May 2026.

Quick reference
 Manage course instances

File
Edit




Add a course instance
data/instances.yml
Copy an existing instance and update its values.


Set the current instance
data/instances.yml
Set status: current for the new instance and status: previous for the old one.


Show or hide a previous instance in the banner
data/instances.yml
Set visible: true or visible: false.


Change the displayed name
data/instances.yml
Change the value of label.


Change the instance order
data/instances.yml
Set sort_key using the format YYYYMM.

text:
5.8 Edit the footer
The footer at the bottom of the landing page contains information about the course page development, its licence, and a link to the course repository on GitHub.

5.8.1 Change the footer text

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file footer.qmd.
Locate:

By SciLifeLab Training Hub. Licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

Built with Quarto and hosted on GitHub Pages.

Replace the text with the information you want to display in the footer.







Tip



If you use a licence other than CC BY 4.0, update both the licence name and its link.
In [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/):

replace the text between [ ] with the name of the licence;
replace the URL between ( ) with the corresponding licence URL.





5.8.2 Change the GitHub repository link
The GitHub logo in the footer links visitors to the course repository.

In the main branch, open the _sections folder and then the file footer.qmd.
Locate:

<a href="https://github.com/SciLifeLab-Training/scilifelab-training-template-staging/tree/main" class="landing-footer__image-link">

Replace only the URL inside href="..." with the URL of your course repository.

For example:
<a href="https://github.com/your-organisation/your-course/tree/main" class="landing-footer__image-link">

title: 7  FAIRification and publishing your course
section: 7.2 Make your materials easy to cite
text:
7.2 Make your materials easy to cite
To make your training easier to cite, you can provide citation information in a CITATION.cff file. This file contains structured information about how your training materials should be cited, including the course title, authors, ORCID identifiers, licence, and links to the course repository and website.

7.2.1 Create the citation file for your course
The SciLifeLab Course Page Template already contains a CITATION.cff file in the root of the repository on the main branch. This file describes the template itself. When you use the template for your own course, replace the contents of CITATION.cff with citation information for your own training materials.

In the main branch, open CITATION.cff.
Delete the existing contents of the file.
Copy and paste the following starter text:

cff-version: 1.2.0
message: "If you use these training materials, please cite them as below."

title: "COURSE TITLE"

authors:
  - family-names: "SURNAME"
    given-names: "GIVEN NAME"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"

license: CC-BY-4.0

repository-code: "https://github.com/ORGANISATION/REPOSITORY"
url: "https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY/"

references:
  - type: software
    title: "SciLifeLab Course Page Template"
    repository-code: "PERMANENT TEMPLATE REPOSITORY URL"

Replace the placeholder values with information about your course.








Field
What to enter




title
The title of your course or training materials.


family-names
The author’s family name or surname.


given-names
The author’s given name(s).


orcid
The author’s ORCID identifier, if they have one.


license
The licence under which the training materials are made available.


repository-code
The URL of the GitHub repository containing your course materials.


url
The URL of the published course website.









Important



Keep:
cff-version: 1.2.0
unchanged. This is the version of the Citation File Format specification, not the version of your course.




7.2.2 Add multiple authors
Add a separate entry under authors for each person who should be credited as an author of the training materials.
For example:
authors:
  - family-names: "Smith"
    given-names: "Anna"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"

  - family-names: "Jones"
    given-names: "David"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"
If an author does not have an ORCID, simply omit the orcid line:
authors:
  - family-names: "Jones"
    given-names: "David"






Tip



ORCID provides researchers with a persistent identifier that distinguishes them from other researchers. If your contributors have ORCID identifiers, include them in CITATION.cff.




7.2.3 Acknowledge this template in your course
The starter file contains the following entry:
references:
  - type: software
    title: "SciLifeLab Course Page Template"
    repository-code: "PERMANENT TEMPLATE REPOSITORY URL"
Keep this entry when adapting CITATION.cff for your course. It acknowledges the SciLifeLab Course Page Template as the resource used to create your course website.


7.2.4 Citation files for individual course instances
How you manage CITATION.cff depends on how you publish your course materials.
If your course is maintained as one continuously updated resource, you can maintain the citation information in the main branch.
If individual course instances are released separately (in this template by adding and publishing branches), their citation information may also differ. For example, different instances may have different contributors.
In this case, update CITATION.cff in the specific course-instance branch before creating the release. This allows the citation metadata for that release to reflect the people and materials associated with that particular course instance.






Tip



Before publishing a course instance, check that CITATION.cff contains the correct title, authors, ORCIDs, licence, repository URL, and course website URL for the materials you are releasing.



Quick reference
 Make your course citable

Edit




Add citation information for your course
CITATION.cff

Add an author

Add an ORCID

Add the author’s ORCID using the orcid field.


Credit an author without an ORCID

Include their name and omit the orcid field.


Cite a particular course instance

Update the citation metadata before creating the release.
